title: Tax Track, Lesson 4: Social, health and unemployment insurance - where does 10.5% of your salary go?
subtitle: The second-largest deduction on your payslip, and what you get for it
whyItMatters: Many people treat the 10.5% for insurance as money lost, when it actually buys pension, healthcare and unemployment entitlements - and the company pays another 21.5% on top for you. Understanding it lets you judge the whole package rather than just the salary figure.
openingQuestion: On the payslip, the employee pays 10.5% towards compulsory insurance. What percentage does the company add on top?
openingOptions: Nothing extra - the employee carries all of it
explanation: Total compulsory insurance is 32% of the contribution salary base: 10.5% from the employee (8% pension, 1.5% health, 1% unemployment) and 21.5% from the company (14% pension, 3% sickness and maternity, 0.5% occupational accident, 3% health, 1% unemployment). The company's share is a real cost it bears for you.

diagram.label: 32% in total into the insurance funds

realWorldExample.description: On a gross salary of 30 million, the company does not spend 30 million. It also pays 21.5% × 30 = 6.45 million in insurance, taking the real cost to 36.45 million a month. Meanwhile the employee receives about 26.2 million. That gap of more than 10 million is something both sides should understand when negotiating pay.

quiz.question: Within the employee's 10.5%, which fund takes the largest share?
options: The pension and survivorship fund (8%)
The health insurance fund (1.5%)
The unemployment insurance fund (1%)
The sickness and maternity benefit fund (3%)
quiz.explanation: 8 of the 10.5 points go to the pension fund - the largest share, and the part that accumulates towards your own pension later.

quiz.question: What is the combined compulsory contribution from both sides?
options: 21% of the contribution salary base
32% of the contribution salary base
10.5% of the contribution salary base
Whatever the company and the employee agree between them
quiz.explanation: 10.5% (employee) + 21.5% (company) = 32%. This is set by law, not a matter for agreement.

quiz.question: Why is compulsory insurance not simply money lost?
options: Because the contributions earn interest like a bank deposit
Because the full amount is refunded when you leave the job
Because it buys pension, healthcare and unemployment entitlements
Because the company refunds the deduction at the end of the year
quiz.explanation: It buys entitlements: a pension in old age, treatment costs covered through health insurance, and support when you lose your job through unemployment insurance.

quiz.question: How does compulsory insurance affect your income tax?
options: It raises taxable income, so you pay more tax
It is credited directly against the tax due
It has no bearing on how income tax is worked out
It comes off income before the tax is calculated
quiz.explanation: Compulsory insurance is deducted before taxable income is worked out, so it both buys entitlements and indirectly lowers your tax.

quiz.question: Why does a contribution base below your real salary hurt you in the long run?
options: Because pensions and benefits are all calculated on what was contributed, not on real pay
Because the tax authority will claw back the difference at the year-end reconciliation
Because employees contributing below their salary lose health insurance cover
Because the company is fined and deducts that fine from the employee's salary
quiz.explanation: Contributing less means more in hand today, but every later entitlement - pension, maternity, unemployment - is calculated on what was contributed. It is a trade between money now and entitlements decades away, and the loss usually stays invisible until the moment you need it.

keyTakeaways: The employee pays 10.5%: 8% pension + 1.5% health + 1% unemployment
The company adds 21.5%, making 32% of the contribution salary base in total
Compulsory insurance is deducted BEFORE income tax is calculated, so it lowers tax indirectly
The contribution salary base is capped - very high salaries do not keep contributing at the same rate forever

practicePrompt.question: Your gross salary is 24 million VND. How much goes into the insurance funds each month, counting both your share and the company's?
options: 2.52 million VND - counting only your own share
5.16 million VND - counting only the company's share
7.68 million VND - 32% of 24 million in total
24 million VND - the whole salary
practicePrompt.explanation: Your share: 24 × 10.5% = 2.52 million. The company's: 24 × 21.5% = 5.16 million. Total into the funds = 24 × 32% = 7.68 million VND a month. The figure shows the real cost of employing you is well above your gross salary.

summary.keyIdea: Employee 10.5% + company 21.5% = 32% of the contribution salary base
summary.commonMistake: Treating the 10.5% as money thrown away, and looking only at gross salary when comparing packages between companies.
summary.action: Check the insurance contribution base on your payslip against your actual gross salary.

application.title: Check your contribution base
application.message: On your payslip, find the line for the social insurance contribution salary. Many companies contribute on a figure below actual gross pay - which lowers the deduction now, but lowers your pension and benefits later too.
application.secondary: It is a trade worth weighing, especially if you have many working years ahead of you.

sections.text: After tax, compulsory insurance is the largest deduction line on a payslip. But unlike tax, it buys you specific entitlements - and the share the company pays for you is twice what you pay yourself.

items: The employee - 10.5% in total: pension and survivorship 8%, health insurance 1.5%, unemployment insurance 1%
The company - 21.5% in total: pension 14%, sickness and maternity 3%, occupational accident and disease 0.5%, health insurance 3%, unemployment insurance 1%
32% of the contribution salary base flows into the insurance funds altogether

left.label: The 'money lost' view
left.text: 10.5% comes off the salary every month, with nothing visibly coming back straight away.

right.label: The 'buying entitlements' view
right.text: It buys a pension in old age, treatment costs covered, and support when you lose your job - and the company puts another 21.5% into the same funds.

sections.text: The double effect on income tax

Compulsory insurance comes off income BEFORE tax is calculated. So besides buying entitlements, it pulls taxable income down and leaves you paying less tax. On a gross salary of 30 million, the 3.15 million of insurance reduces taxable income by exactly that amount.

sections.label: Beware a low contribution base
sections.text: Some companies contribute on a salary lower than what they actually pay. Less is deducted from you now, but pensions, unemployment support and maternity benefits are all calculated on what was contributed - so the long-run loss usually outweighs the short-run gain.

concepts.def: The pension, survivorship, sickness and maternity funds - the backbone of your later pension
Covers part of the cost of medical examination and treatment, as prescribed
Support payments and job-search help when you lose your job

concepts.vi: Tiền lương làm căn cứ đóng
concepts.def: The salary the contributions are calculated on, subject to a regulated cap

lines: The 10.5% does not vanish - it turns into entitlements, and into a lower tax bill.
